cards.front: Why can a bacterium make a human protein such as insulin from a human gene?
cards.back: The **genetic code** is almost universal, so the same base sequence codes for the same amino acids in almost all organisms.
cards.hint: Consider whether a bacterium reads a human gene in the same way a human cell does.

cards.front: What are the steps for joining a human gene into a plasmid?
cards.back: 1) The same **restriction enzyme** cuts the human DNA and the plasmid, leaving matching single-stranded ends. 2) The ends pair by complementary base pairing. 3) **DNA ligase** joins the sugar–phosphate backbones.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to both DNA samples before anything is joined.

cards.front: Why is a marker gene included on the plasmid?
cards.back: It lets scientists find the **few cells that took up the plasmid**. For example, an antibiotic resistance gene means only those cells survive on agar containing the antibiotic.
cards.hint: Most treated cells stay unchanged, so how could the rest be picked out?

cards.front: A student says restriction enzymes join the human gene into the plasmid. What is wrong?
cards.back: **Restriction enzymes** only cut DNA at a specific base sequence. Joining the fragments is the job of **DNA ligase**.
cards.hint: Check what each enzyme in the process actually does.

cards.back: A small **circular loop of DNA** in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome, that can be passed to new cells.
cards.hint: Compare where it sits with the main chromosome.

cards.back: DNA formed by **joining DNA from two different sources**.
cards.hint: Think about where the human gene and the plasmid each come from.

cards.front: Which conditions does a fermenter keep at their best values?
cards.back: **Temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrient supply**. Stirring spreads nutrients and oxygen to every cell.
cards.hint: Think about what a growing culture needs in order to thrive.

cards.front: Why must other microorganisms be kept out of a fermenter?
cards.back: They would **compete for nutrients** and could spoil the product.
cards.hint: Think about what happens when two organisms share the same food supply.

cards.front: What happens to the protein after the bacteria have made it?
cards.back: It is **separated from the culture and purified**. Purity matters because many such drugs are injected into patients.
cards.hint: Think about what must happen before a drug reaches a patient.

cards.front: Why are some human proteins made in cultured mammalian cells instead of bacteria?
cards.back: Some proteins need **sugar groups added** after they are made, and bacteria cannot do this.
cards.hint: Consider what changes some proteins undergo after they are assembled.

cards.back: The use of **genetically modified animals or plants** to make pharmaceutical products.
cards.hint: Think of the goats and the leaves mentioned in the note.

cards.front: Which host is used to make Factor VIII?
cards.back: **Cultured mammalian cells**. Factor VIII helps blood to clot in haemophilia.
cards.hint: Look at the table of drugs and the hosts that make them.

cards.front: Which drug is secreted in the milk of GM goats?
cards.back: **Antithrombin**, which reduces clots in people who lack it.
cards.hint: Think about which host in the table produces a drug in its milk.

cards.front: Why is a DNA copy of mRNA used for some human genes instead of the gene itself?
cards.back: Human genes contain **introns**, which bacteria cannot remove, so the protein would be wrong. A DNA copy made by **reverse transcriptase** has no introns.
cards.hint: Think about the non-coding sections found inside human genes.
